Integrity detection after content has been shown to the user or acted upon is much weaker than detection before use. Requiring the claim to state when detection occurs exposes designs that only detect tampering retrospectively.

A production claim must be self-contained and evaluable: property, scope, asset, threats, composites, phases, prerequisites, limitations and evidence class. Missing fields leave room for readers to assume broader protection.

Unlinkability depends on exactly which items must not be correlated and what side information the observer has. Without this, timing or IP data could link items while the claim still appears satisfied.

Rollback resistance applies to particular state (counters, ledgers, checkpoints) via a particular mechanism (hardware counter, transparency). Naming both lets reviewers check that the mechanism actually covers the state.

Unsigned protocols can still produce transferable evidence through MACs with long-term keys, server logs or metadata. Deniability requires analysis of what a third party can verify, not just absence of signatures.
Where a composite scenario changes a property's outcome, silence would be read as coverage. Declaring the property's status for that composite makes the effect of combined threats explicit.

Properties legitimately differ by threat (confidentiality against a passive network but not a compromised endpoint). Allowing per-threat status keeps claims honest rather than forcing all-or-nothing statements.

Recovery confidentiality depends on which authorities, secrets, services and hardware are involved and what history recovery can expose. Naming them shows whether, for example, a provider-held escrow can restore message history.

Message authenticity convinces the recipient of the sender but may be deniable to others. Treating it as transferable proof would misrepresent its legal or evidentiary weight unless non-repudiation is separately claimed.

Claims often depend on assumptions outside the E2EESA invariants (honest hardware, correct clock, user verification). Enumerating them lets users and assessors see what must hold for the claim to be valid.
If a required dimension (e.g. exposure window) is missing, filling it with a default would invent a claim the profile never made. Treating omissions as unspecified keeps interpretation fail-closed.
Unknown property IDs cannot be interpreted against shared definitions and may hide invented or misspelled properties. Rejecting them keeps claims within the registered vocabulary.
Limitations (e.g. no protection for previews, sparse PQ healing) are as important as the property. Recording them prevents claims being consumed without their caveats.

Claims are bounded by their declared fields. Reading them more broadly, for example applying a device-level claim to the account or a steady-state claim to post-compromise, creates unearned assurance.
'Metadata protected' is meaningless without saying which fields (contacts, timing, IPs, sizes) and what protection. The phrase otherwise implies broad privacy that content E2EE does not provide.

No system remains available against an adversary that can block all communication forever. Claiming general availability in that model is false, so availability claims must be bounded to realistic adversaries.

Signature checks stop unsigned tampering but not a malicious update the vendor signed. Stating whether that case is in scope reveals whether additional controls like transparency or reproducible builds are needed.
Properties like FS and PCS only make sense relative to a compromise event. Using defined phases makes it explicit when each property holds and avoids blanket statements.
Healing requires fresh secrets the attacker cannot see; while the attacker controls the endpoint it sees them too. Presenting PCS as protection during live control would be false.

Key consistency applies to a specific object (key directory, group state, log) and may prevent inconsistency or only detect it later. Stating both determines whether users are protected before or after harm.

Deniability and non-repudiation are opposites for the same evidence. Claiming both under the same scope is contradictory; separating scopes (e.g. deniable chat, non-repudiable signed documents) keeps each meaningful.
Authenticating a device is not authenticating a person or account. Stating the principal granularity prevents a device-level guarantee being read as proof of who is using it.

Confidentiality against the provider must hold both when it passively reads data and when it actively deviates. Stating coverage of each makes clear whether an active provider (e.g. key substitution) is defended against.

An attacker with live endpoint access reads messages as they are decrypted; ratcheting cannot protect them. Claiming FS against live compromise because a ratchet exists confuses protection of past keys with protection of current plaintext.
FS and PCS are defined around compromise events; expressing them as steady-state hides the intervals in which they do not hold. Compromise-aware phases make their temporal limits explicit.

Harvest-now and active quantum adversaries threaten different things, and a single remaining classical component can defeat confidentiality. Stating coverage and classical dependencies prevents partial PQ deployments being over-labelled.

Minimisation is relative to which metadata and which observer. Without stating them, reducing logs on one server could be presented as broad metadata minimisation while other observers still see everything.
Downgrade resistance protects a specific negotiated object (version, suite, profile) relative to a minimum policy. Identifying both shows what cannot be downgraded and who set the floor.
Backups use different keys, storage and access paths than live channels. Live E2EE says nothing about whether the backup provider can read history, so backup confidentiality needs its own analysis.

Confidentiality against quantum adversaries does not prevent them forging classical signatures to impersonate peers. Keeping PQ confidentiality and PQ authentication separate prevents misinterpreting hybrid KEM deployments.

PCS is useful only if users know what heals, when, after how long, what honest activity is needed and what blocks it. Requiring these fields makes PCS claims testable and reveals conditions like idle peers or dropped messages that delay healing.

Encrypting content leaves routing, timing and relationship metadata visible. Interpreting content confidentiality as metadata confidentiality would misinform users whose risk comes from contact graphs.
Marketing often rounds claims up ('military-grade', 'fully private'). Prohibiting broadening beyond recorded limitations keeps public statements consistent with the evaluated claim.

Non-repudiation requires evidence a third party can verify, a binding to a real identity and trusted keys. Naming these elements shows whether the evidence would actually stand up outside the conversation.
A provided or conditional claim without a threat or asset has no testable content. Requiring at least one of each gives the claim a concrete subject and adversary.

Replay resistance must say what object is protected and how duplicates, reordering and rollback are handled, since these differ (out-of-order delivery is legitimate; duplicates are not). Otherwise claims may cover messages but not, say, group operations.

Sender-hidden credentials authenticate a sender to the recipient without the service seeing who sent. If they outlive device revocation, a stolen or revoked device could keep sending authenticated messages indefinitely; lifecycle must follow the identity architecture.

Calls use different signalling and media paths (TURN servers, ICE candidates) that expose IPs and call graphs. A messaging metadata result does not cover them, so extending it to calls would overstate privacy.

Each prohibited behaviour turns the delivery service into a surveillance system: durable social graphs, content-derived classifications, cross-service identifiers and over-retained routing data. Forbidding them limits what a breached or compelled service can disclose.

Abuse controls are needed, but if they quietly required sender identity while the product still reported sender-hidden conformance, users would believe their identity was hidden when it was not. Any change of mode must be reflected in conformance.

OHTTP's privacy relies on splitting knowledge: the relay sees the IP but not the request, the gateway sees the request but not the IP, and the sender identity is inside E2EE. This only works if relay and gateway are administratively independent; otherwise they can trivially join their views.
OHTTP encapsulation uses HPKE; using unregistered or weak KEM, KDF or AEAD choices would undermine the request confidentiality that the relay partition depends on.
Delivery metadata that is never collected or quickly deleted cannot be breached, subpoenaed or misused. Minimisation is the baseline every profile must meet before stronger mechanisms are layered on.
Headers such as Forwarded or Via, or relay-added pseudonyms, would hand the gateway exactly the client-identifying information OHTTP is designed to withhold, collapsing the partition.

If an attacker can substitute the gateway key configuration, the client encrypts to the attacker, who can then read requests. Authenticating the configuration ensures encapsulation reaches the intended gateway.

When the service does not see the sender, only the recipient can authenticate it, and must do so from material inside the E2EE envelope; otherwise anyone could impersonate any sender to the recipient.

Under relay partitioning the IP address is the main link back to the person. Zero durable retention after completion means a later breach or legal demand cannot recover which clients sent which requests.

Metadata claims are only checkable if each delivery records which profile applied and what was actually visible and retained. The listed evidence lets assessors confirm privacy behaviour rather than trust configuration claims.

Sender-hidden delivery still reveals recipients and timing to the service, from which relationships can often be inferred. Unqualified 'hides who is messaging whom' claims would mislead high-risk users.
Operators need aggregate counters for capacity and abuse management. Permitting them only in forms that cannot reconstruct per-user histories balances operations against minimisation.

These concrete bounds make the minimised-metadata profile testable: metadata and IPs deleted within 24 hours, no durable relationship records, and no service access to content. Concrete limits stop 'minimal' from meaning indefinite.

Reusing an HPKE context with changed plaintext could leak information or cause nonce reuse, and lets the relay or gateway correlate retries. A fresh context per changed request preserves confidentiality and unlinkability.

A global passive observer can correlate traffic entering the relay with traffic leaving the gateway, and colluding relay and gateway can join their logs. The relay-partitioned profile does not defend against either, so it must not claim to.
Selecting a metadata profile changes routing, not trust in content. If it caused plaintext to reach the service, relay or gateway, metadata privacy would be bought by sacrificing content E2EE.
OHTTP and relays protect metadata in transit but are not end-to-end encryption between users. Replacing or terminating the pairwise/group layer would expose content to the gateway or service.
Clients need the gateway key configuration. RFC 9540 or another authenticated channel may supply it, but a channel that identifies the client to the gateway would defeat the relay partition.

The stricter minimised profile shortens retention to one hour and forbids relationship records. A shorter window reduces how much a breach or compelled disclosure can reveal about recent communication.

OHTTP does not itself prevent replay of encapsulated requests, and the gateway cannot see who sent them. Application-level replay protection stops a relay or observer from re-submitting messages to cause duplicate delivery.

Sender-hidden credentials replace service-visible identity, so they must be verified by the receiving endpoint and tied to valid identity/device state; otherwise revoked or fabricated senders could pass as authorised.
Padding buckets trade bandwidth and latency for anonymity-set size. Allowing deployment-specific choices, guided by the required anonymity set, lets products tune cost without abandoning size hiding.
The service must still prevent arbitrary parties from delivering to a recipient. Demonstrating authorisation without revealing the sender's account preserves both spam control and sender privacy.

Abuse control usually requires knowing who sends. A recipient-scoped capability lets the service enforce authorisation and rate limits without learning the sender's account identity, reconciling abuse prevention with sender privacy.
Sharing per-request logs between relay and gateway would reproduce the joined view the partition exists to prevent, even if each party individually behaves correctly.

A gateway could issue each client a unique key configuration and then recognise them by which key decrypts their requests. Rejecting personalised configurations prevents the key itself becoming a tracking identifier.

Delivery capabilities stand in for sender identity, so they must not become a new identifier: recipient-scoping prevents cross-recipient correlation, avoiding stable cross-service use prevents tracking, rotation on block cuts off unwanted senders, and protection limits misuse.
If the recipient trusted the service's claimed sender identifier, a malicious service could attribute messages to anyone. The credential must be verified cryptographically by the recipient.
Abuse-specific routing or challenges can single out some clients, shrinking the crowd they hide in. Products must not claim unlinkability stronger than their actual relay behaviour provides.
Replay detection can use various identifiers or time windows; the requirement is outcome-based so implementations can choose, but a replay must never trigger duplicate security-sensitive processing.
Without a relay, the service sees the client's IP on every connection. Sender-hidden delivery hides account identity, not network location, and claims must not suggest otherwise.
Encapsulated request sizes can reveal message length or type to the relay and network observers. Padding to buckets reduces this side channel within the relay-partitioned design.

A hardware token only bounds key exposure if no other usable copy can exist. Cloning, admin duplication, backup objects or vendor recovery each create an extra copy that an attacker could target; documenting them reveals whether 'single-device' protection is real.

Keeping the previous vault generation helps recover from a crash mid-write, but an attacker could present it to roll state back. It is allowed only when the product can tell genuine crash recovery from rollback within its policy.

A torn write could leave a vault that partly authenticates or is unreadable, causing loss of keys or acceptance of corrupted state. Atomic replacement guarantees each committed generation is complete.

These baseline rules ensure every storage profile, hardware or not, encrypts with an approved AEAD, authenticates before use, tracks generations, never exports or syncs the raw root key and never leaves plaintext secrets at rest. They define the minimum below which no profile is acceptable.

The software profile may opportunistically use hardware, but because it is not required, no hardware-dependent property is claimed. This prevents opportunistic use being presented as a hardware guarantee.

Encoding use restrictions (purpose, algorithm, auth requirement) in the keystore means even compromised application code cannot use the key for other operations, narrowing the impact of an app-level compromise.

The Secure Enclave only performs certain operations (e.g. P-256 ECDH/signing); other secrets sit outside, encrypted. Documenting the split shows which secrets enjoy enclave protection and which are exposed to OS compromise.
The rollback anchor must move forward with the vault; otherwise an old vault would still match the anchor and rollback could not be detected.

Storing an exportable private key in the Keychain is very different from having the Secure Enclave generate and hold it. Only the latter provides non-exportability; using the wrong API would silently drop the hardware guarantee.

On Android, requesting hardware backing does not guarantee it; devices may fall back to software. Inspecting the actual key security level prevents claiming TEE or StrongBox protection the device did not provide.
Local authentication gates reduce misuse by someone holding an unlocked or stolen device. Allowing policies to require them lets products match local-access threats to usability needs.
Without an anchor, an attacker who restores an older vault copy cannot be detected. Claiming rollback resistance in that configuration would be false.
A hardware token used without PIN or presence lets malware on the host use it silently while plugged in. Requiring explicit authorisation per sensitive use limits that abuse.
Key attestation proves properties of a key in a security module, not that the app, OS or user is trustworthy. Over-interpreting it would let a compromised device pass as healthy.
Policies may accept weaker storage on some devices, but evidence must show the profile actually used so that assessments and users are not told a stronger boundary is in place.
The vault is only as strong as the key protecting it. Binding its protection to the selected profile ensures the advertised boundary (software, TEE, enclave, token) actually guards the vault key.

Backing up vault ciphertext is safe only if the backup cannot also obtain the key that decrypts it. Shipping the raw root key with the ciphertext would make the backup provider able to read all local secrets.
Creating or importing the root key as non-extractable within the token's model ensures it cannot later be read out by host software, which is the property hardware tokens are used for.
If any required protection cannot be established and the implementation continues anyway, users get a weaker boundary under a stronger label. Failing closed keeps claims tied to reality.

Platform keystores behave differently across OS versions and vendors. Testing and documenting the chosen platform's real behaviour prevents assumptions copied from documentation from standing in for evidence.

Ratchet and session state change constantly and cannot all live in hardware. An authenticated encrypted vault with a 256-bit key gives that state strong at-rest protection while hardware guards only the vault key.
The root or wrapping key is the high-value secret; if it can leave the hardware boundary, an attacker with temporary access can copy it and decrypt the vault offline later.

Hardware may prevent copying a key yet still let malware use it while the device is unlocked. Distinguishing extraction resistance from use-authorisation abuse prevents non-exportability being mistaken for protection against live misuse.
Keeping only the root key in hardware and using it to unwrap a software vault gives hardware protection to the most valuable secret while allowing flexible protocol state handling.

Attestation can be forged or stale unless the full chain, security level, key attributes, app binding, firmware version and revocation are checked against policy. Partial checks accept emulators or revoked devices.
Syncing a raw root key turns a per-device secret into a shared one held by the sync channel and every device, so compromise of any of them exposes all vaults.
Trusting attestation without validating chain, security level, key properties and revocation lets attackers present software keys or revoked hardware as trusted.
A TPM NV counter lives outside the vault and cannot be rolled back with it, making it a suitable anchor when correctly authorised.

Keys can be invalidated by biometric changes or OS resets. Silently escrowing or exporting the root key to avoid this would destroy non-exportability; recovery must use the defined recovery or reauthorisation flows.
The software profile has no hardware boundary, so claiming isolation or non-exportability would misrepresent how easily an attacker with device access can copy keys.
Silent fallback from requested hardware to software is a downgrade that users cannot see. The profile must not be claimed when the stronger boundary was not obtained.
TPM keys can be created with attributes that permit duplication or with weak authorisation. Correct attributes and policy are what prevent extraction through normal interfaces.
Copying a hardware key into app memory exposes it to memory scraping and crash dumps, negating the hardware protection. Using operation handles keeps the key inside the boundary.

Long-lived identity and recovery keys are most damaging if misused from a stolen unlocked device. Requiring recent unlock or authentication for these operations narrows that window at acceptable usability cost.
Argon2id below RFC 9106 floors makes offline guessing of passphrase-protected vaults cheap. Enforcing a recommended floor sets a minimum attacker cost for stolen vault files.
Users may assume a KDF makes any passphrase safe. Documenting that Argon2id only raises guessing cost prevents a weak passphrase being mistaken for strong protection.
Monotonic generations give every durable change a position in an ordered history so the rollback anchor can detect an older vault being restored.

Storage claims involve many separable mechanisms (profile, AEAD, non-exportability, real security level, attestation, auth policy, authenticated load, rollback, rotation). Demonstrating each avoids a claim resting on configuration intent rather than observed behaviour.
Synchronising vault backups changes who can decrypt them and how recovery works. Tying this to the recovery profile ensures backups do not create an unreviewed recovery path.

Any code running in the app process (including malware via injection) has process access. If policy requires explicit user presence, treating process access as presence would let such code bypass the user.
Invalidating the old key before rewrapping could lose the vault; rewrapping first preserves availability. Emergency handling may deliberately destroy access when compromise risk outweighs data loss.
Per-device root keys mean a compromise of one device does not expose the others and each device can be revoked independently.

Android TEE and StrongBox provide hardware isolation when attestation confirms the security level. Accepting verified evidence for either lets products use widely available TEEs without overclaiming StrongBox.

Each trigger (suspected compromise, failing attestation, auth-policy change, ownership reset, platform migration) means the old key's trust assumptions no longer hold, so continuing to use it would carry forward an invalid boundary.
Secrets leak via copies, dumps, swap, logs and temp files far more often than via cryptanalysis. Avoiding these paths reduces exposure to forensic and crash-report collection.
StrongBox, TEE and software differ greatly in attack resistance. When fallback occurs, evidence must reflect the boundary actually achieved so users and assessors are not misinformed.
Sealing to PCRs can prevent use under tampered boot states but adds fragility across updates. Making it optional lets deployments choose it where the boot-chain threat justifies the operational cost.
For token-bound profiles, making the vault unusable when the token is absent is a deliberate security property, ensuring device theft without the token does not expose secrets.
A hardware profile is only established by authoritative evidence of the boundary and key attributes; without verifying it, the implementation is trusting its own request.
A generated unlock secret with fewer than 128 random bits can be brute-forced offline from a stolen vault. 128 bits places guessing beyond practical reach independent of the KDF.
Some APIs accept non-exportable flags but ignore them on certain devices. Verifying the platform actually marks the key non-exportable ensures the property exists rather than being assumed.
If a superseded key remained usable after rotation, an attacker holding it could still decrypt or produce valid vault data, defeating the purpose of rotating.
The longer plaintext secrets sit in ordinary memory, the more chances memory disclosure, swapping or dumps have to capture them. Short lifetimes reduce that window.
If the anchor is stored alongside the vault, restoring an old disk image restores the old anchor too, and rollback goes undetected. The anchor must live where vault rollback cannot reach it.

Client-side AEAD encryption under the generation BDEK is what keeps backup content unreadable and tamper-evident to the storage provider; server-side or unauthenticated encryption would let the provider read or alter history.
An attacker or storage provider could offer an older backup that lacks recent revocations or contains superseded keys. Comparing against the latest authenticated generation detects such rollback.
In hardware-assisted recovery the hardware only releases a wrapping secret; if it saw the user secret or unwrapped BDEK, a compromised HSM operator could recover backups alone.
Recovery must keep the service outside the content trust boundary. Receiving restored plaintext or the unwrapped BDEK would give it full access to the recovered history.
Without the exact Argon2id and HKDF parameters, a later client cannot reproduce the derivation and the backup becomes unrecoverable; storing them also documents the attacker's guessing cost.
A fresh 256-bit random BDEK per generation ensures each backup has an independent, unguessable key, so compromise of one generation's key does not expose others.
Passphrase-protected backups are vulnerable to offline guessing once copied. Following usability guidance improves passphrase quality, and documenting the weaker boundary sets correct expectations.

Backup security spans many mechanisms (profile, algorithms, key freshness, manifest binding, no server key access, no secret upload, KDF parameters, rollback checks, device authorisation). Demonstrating each prevents a working restore being mistaken for a secure one.
Reusing a BDEK across generations links them cryptographically and means a deleted generation's key still decrypts newer data, defeating rotation and crypto-erasure.
Any of plaintext, recovery secret or unwrapped BDEK lets the service decrypt the backup. Keeping all three away from it preserves end-to-end protection for backups.

Authenticating identity, profile, generation, algorithm, key id, object list and format prevents a provider from swapping objects between backups, mixing generations or downgrading algorithms without detection.
Derived keys and plaintext staging buffers left in memory can be captured by later memory compromise. Prompt erasure reduces this residual exposure.
Monotonic generation numbers make rollback detectable, and tying full replacement to a new generation guarantees BDEK rotation on each replacement.

Undetected changes to identity, generation, algorithm or object set would allow cross-account restores, rollback or downgrade. The authentication construction must make such changes cryptographically detectable.

The recovery secret is the only barrier against offline guessing of a stolen backup. Argon2id v0x13 with ≥16-byte salt and RFC 9106 floor parameters ensures each guess has substantial memory and time cost.
Multiple replicas of one wrapping key fail together and are not a threshold scheme. Claiming threshold recovery for replication would overstate resistance to a single compromised operator.
Checksums help users transcribe codes correctly but are deterministic from the secret; counting them as entropy would overstate resistance to guessing.
Restoring a stale generation could reinstate revoked keys or deleted data. The normal restore path must refuse it; any deliberate historical access goes through a separate export feature.

Backups and recovery are common back doors around E2EE. No non-recipient (storage, recovery service, hardware operator) may alone be able to recover plaintext, preserving the E2EE property for stored history.
Releasing restored plaintext before the manifest is authenticated lets a provider feed unverified or substituted content into the client, which may act on it before detection.
Users may prefer a memorable passphrase. It is permitted, but only with the documented weaker offline-guessing boundary and Argon2id protections.
E2EE backups can become unrecoverable if secrets are lost. Products must document this rather than quietly adding server-side recovery that would undermine confidentiality.
AEAD nonce reuse under one key can break confidentiality and allow forgeries. Nonce construction must satisfy the selected AEAD's requirements across all chunks and objects.
Backups still reveal sizes, timing and account linkage to the storage provider. Implying metadata confidentiality would misstate what encrypted backups hide.
Because content is client-encrypted and authenticated, the storage location need not be trusted. This permission reflects the design goal that providers hold only ciphertext.
A generated recovery secret with at least 128 random bits resists offline guessing even if KDF costs are reduced, giving a strong baseline independent of user behaviour.
If the service alone says which generation is latest, it can present a stale one as current. The client must have an independent source such as local state or authenticated recovery state.

Possessing the backup secret should not be enough to become a trusted endpoint; otherwise an attacker who obtains it could add a device. Device authorisation must already exist before history is released.
An unwrapped BDEK held by the storage service lets the service decrypt the backup directly. It must only ever be stored wrapped.
A user-chosen passphrase typically has far less than 128 bits of entropy, even with Argon2id. Claiming equivalence would mislead users about how easily stolen backups can be cracked.
A server-restorable history that remains decryptable after all endpoints lose keys means the server effectively holds decryption authority, which contradicts end-to-end encryption.
Recovery material kept for a deleted generation can still decrypt any surviving copies. Destroying it supports cryptographic erasure.
Using raw Argon2id output directly as an AEAD key risks cross-use with other derivations. Domain separation through HKDF gives a key bound to the recovery-envelope purpose.
Crypto-erasure only works if every copy of the key is destroyed. Stating which replicas, hardware keys and user secrets are assumed destroyed makes the erasure claim verifiable.

Hardware-assisted recovery is only stronger than a server secret if the wrapping key is non-exportable, its lifecycle and boundary are documented, attestation is verified, and release requests are authorised and rate-limited.
Historical export is legitimate but carries rollback risk. Keeping it separate and preventing it from rolling security state backward stops it being used to reinstate revoked keys or states.

A fresh random 256-bit key per attachment makes each file's protection independent and prevents confirmation-of-file attacks that deterministic or convergent encryption allow, where the service learns whether a user stores a known file.
Giving new members historical attachment keys on join would expose files shared before they were present, violating join confidentiality unless an explicit history-sharing action authorises it.
Removed members must not be able to open attachments sent afterwards. Excluding them from new attachment-key distribution enforces removal confidentiality for files.

Attachment security depends on precise mechanisms: fresh keys, exact manifest digest, correct chunking, exact nonce construction, AAD binding, verify-before-release and E2EE-only key distribution. Each must be demonstrated since any one failing breaks confidentiality or integrity.

Filename, media type, plaintext hash and key are sensitive; if storage required them, they would leak to the provider. Keeping them only in the E2EE private manifest preserves attachment metadata confidentiality.
Independent chunk handling enables resumable and seekable transfers for large files; it is safe because each chunk is authenticated against the manifest, which must be obtained first.

The storage service is untrusted; it holds only ciphertext. Delivering the key and manifest solely inside authenticated E2EE messages to authorised devices ensures only intended recipients can decrypt.
Uploads abandoned before a parent message is sent would otherwise accumulate indefinitely, wasting storage and retaining ciphertext and metadata longer than needed. Bounded cleanup limits both.
Users expect deletion to remove stored copies. Requesting removal from primary storage and known caches per documented rules makes deletion meaningful while being honest about retention limits.
Bounded chunk sizes keep per-chunk memory and AEAD limits reasonable, and exact sizing for all but the last chunk prevents ambiguity that could enable truncation or extension attacks.
URLs, query strings, CDN metadata, logs and analytics are all routinely visible to infrastructure and third parties. A key appearing in any of them would let those parties decrypt the attachment.
A malicious storage service could reorder, swap or cut chunks to alter the file. Requiring validation failure in all these cases ensures the recipient never accepts a modified file.
An exact chunk-count formula lets recipients detect truncated or padded files; the zero-length special case avoids ambiguity for empty files.
Once a recipient holds a key or plaintext, the sender cannot force its deletion. Claiming global recall would mislead users about the effectiveness of 'unsend' or expiry.
Per-chunk authentication proves each chunk is genuine but a whole-file hash check additionally confirms the reassembled file matches what the sender intended, catching logic errors in reassembly.

Thumbnails, transcripts and OCR output reveal attachment content. Uploading them unprotected or under the parent key reuse would leak content; they must stay local or be separate fresh-key attachments.
Binding attachment id, manifest digest, chunk index, count and length into each chunk's AEAD ties every chunk to one position in one file, so chunks cannot be moved between files or positions.
These are the concrete attacks a storage provider can attempt with ciphertext alone. Requiring each to fail closes the gaps between per-chunk encryption and whole-file integrity.

Parsers and renderers are a major attack surface; feeding them unauthenticated bytes lets a provider deliver exploit payloads. Authenticating each chunk before release keeps attacker-controlled data out of parsers.
If some manifest field were not covered by the digest, it could be altered without detection, for example changing the declared length or media type.
Distributing the key to stale device state could include revoked devices or miss new ones. Using current authorised state limits decryption to the devices that should have access.
Delivering the key and manifest inside an E2EE message inherits that channel's authentication and confidentiality, so attachments are as protected as the conversation they belong to.

In the confidential-compute profile, identifiers are protected only inside the attested enclave; if the host OS, hypervisor or orchestration saw them, the provider would learn users' address books despite the attestation.

Stale directory snapshots may still list users who have since disabled discovery or rotated keys. Expiring them and detecting rollback to old epochs prevents a provider from serving outdated discovery state.
Users who opt out of being found must not be discoverable by any profile; otherwise discovery becomes an enumeration tool against people who explicitly declined it.
VOPRF outputs depend on the server key; without explicit key identifiers and epochs, clients cannot tell which key produced a directory or detect substitution during rotation.

Phone numbers and emails live in small enumerable spaces, so plain or truncated hashes are reversed by brute force. Uploading them is equivalent to uploading the raw address book and cannot be called private discovery.

If clients and directory builders normalise identifiers differently, legitimate matches are missed or attacker-crafted forms match the wrong user. One normalisation profile per epoch keeps matching exact.
The trusted code sees all queried identifiers; returning anything beyond the allowed intersection (e.g. extra users or attributes) would leak directory data to the querying client.

Discovery privacy claims are only checkable with evidence of profile, normalisation version, batch size, policy enforcement and absence of raw or unkeyed uploads; otherwise assessors must trust configuration.

Returning profile data or extra attributes in discovery responses turns discovery into a lookup service. Limiting responses to match bits and minimum bootstrap data keeps identity resolution in the E2EE flow.
A client with enough query budget can test every identifier in a small space no matter how private the protocol is. Claims must acknowledge this limit instead of promising enumeration resistance.
Opt-out must hold even against someone who already knows the identifier; otherwise opt-out only hides users from strangers while still confirming their presence to stalkers who know their number.

Sending identifiers to an enclave is only safe after verifying its attestation chain, checking the measured code against an allowlist, binding the session to that instance and refusing plaintext fallback; skipping any step sends identifiers to unverified code.
Persisted query identifiers create a durable record of who searched for whom, which a breach or subpoena could expose. Not persisting them limits exposure to the request lifetime.
Binding normalisation version, VOPRF key, epoch, snapshot version and authentication data lets clients detect when a directory was built under a different key or rolled back.
Discovery protocols hide identifiers but not the client's IP address. Combining with a metadata-privacy transport is how products needing network-location privacy close that gap.
Attestation verifies code identity, not resistance to side channels such as cache timing. Claiming otherwise would overstate the enclave's protection of identifiers.
In the handle-lookup profile, batching would let a client test many guesses per request. A batch size of one makes rate limits correspond directly to guesses.
Since the service evaluates the VOPRF online, an unlimited budget lets a client enumerate identifiers. An explicit budget or equivalent abuse control bounds enumeration.
Publishing pseudorandom VOPRF-derived tags lets clients check membership offline after evaluating their own identifiers, while tags reveal nothing without server-key evaluation.
Discovery only says an account exists; it does not authenticate keys. Requiring the normal identity, verification and transparency flow prevents a discovery match being treated as a verified peer.
Uploading the raw address book reveals the user's entire social graph, including non-users, to the provider. Private discovery exists to avoid exactly this.
Changing normalisation changes which keys identifiers map to; reusing the old version would make old and new directories inconsistent and cause mismatches or wrong matches.
Extra results such as suggestions, similarity scores or unrequested matches leak social-graph information about other users. Returning only what was asked keeps discovery a narrow lookup.
A discoverability change that takes effect indefinitely late leaves users exposed after opting out. A documented maximum delay bounds that window.
Batch size and per-account evaluation limits are the parameters that bound enumeration. Defining both makes the abuse controls concrete and testable.
Outputs under one VOPRF key do not correspond to tags under another; mixing them causes false negatives or lets a server use a separate key to target users. Proof, key and snapshot must match.
The VOPRF proof shows the server used the committed key; without verifying it, a server could use a per-user key to tag and track specific queries.
A versioned normalisation profile documents exactly how identifiers become discovery keys so clients, directories and auditors agree.
Membership tags derive from the server key; after rotation old tags no longer match new evaluations, and retaining them would let the compromised old key still identify members.
Different membership structures suit different scales; any deterministic authenticated structure is acceptable as long as it supports authenticated membership checks.
Discoverability can differ by mode (phone, email, handle). Positive results only for users whose policy allows that mode prevents one opt-in leaking presence under another identifier.
Query plaintext left in reusable enclave memory can be exposed to later requests or memory-disclosure bugs. Prompt erasure limits that exposure.
An unauthenticated snapshot can be modified to hide or add members. Clients must verify authentication before relying on it for discovery results.
In handle lookup the service sees the queried handle, so the profile only minimises address-book upload. Stating this prevents an overclaim of query secrecy.
Users must trust the attested code; reproducible builds let third parties confirm the measured binary matches reviewed source.
Memorable handles are guessable; the protocol cannot make enumeration hard if the space is small. Products must not imply cryptographic enumeration resistance for such handles.
SFrame base keys let holders decrypt media. If the SFU or signalling server received them, media E2EE would reduce to trusting the conferencing provider.
Releasing unauthenticated media to decoders, recorders or analysis lets an SFU inject crafted frames that exploit decoders or spoof speech. Authentication must precede any consumer.

If semantics vary within a stream or interpretation metadata is unauthenticated, an SFU could cause frames to be decoded differently than intended. Consistent semantics with authenticated metadata prevent reinterpretation.
SFrame uses CTR as nonce; if a crash rolls it back, the next frames reuse key/nonce pairs, breaking confidentiality and authenticity. Persisting CTR before use prevents reuse.
Restarting CTR under the same key after process resumption reuses nonces. A resumed process must continue the counter or rotate keys.

Media E2EE depends on the exact suite, both encryption layers, no SFU key access, distinct sender keys, replay rejection, rotation and membership rekey. Demonstrating each prevents a working call being mistaken for a secure one.
Forwarding a call is not a reason to read it. Any relay, SFU or terminator receiving keys or plaintext would be able to record or alter media.
Accepting a lower media epoch would let an attacker replay an old membership state, re-admitting removed devices to key derivation.
Key lifetime and frame-count bounds limit how much media one key protects and stay within AEAD usage limits. Rotating at the bound keeps both exposure and cryptographic limits in check.
Every device holding a media key can decrypt the call; if it is not represented in authorisation state, users cannot see or control who is listening.
A rejoining device's previous sender key may have been exposed while it was absent. Treating it as new with fresh keys prevents reuse of possibly compromised keying.
Media is as sensitive as messages; every frame must be encrypted and authenticated end-to-end or the SFU can see or alter call content.
A new epoch reflects a membership change; sender keys that persisted across it could still be held by removed participants. All senders must rekey.
After compromise, old sender keys, replay checkpoints and authority may be in attacker hands. Reauthorised devices must start fresh rather than resume as if nothing happened.
Server-side recording of an E2EE call would require the server to decrypt, breaking E2EE silently. Recording must be visible and go through an authorised participant.
Two senders sharing one base key would collide in CTR space and allow cross-sender nonce reuse and impersonation.
Periodic rotation limits exposure from a single key; reusing a KID with a new key confuses receivers about which key applies. Fresh key and fresh KID keep rotation unambiguous.
A removed bot retains whatever keys it held; without rekeying it could continue decrypting the call.
Each (key, KID, CTR) tuple determines the AEAD nonce; using it twice breaks confidentiality and enables forgeries.
An SFU can replay old frames to inject repeated audio or video. Receivers must remember enough per-sender state to reject duplicates within the reorder window.
When the SFU terminates SRTP/DTLS, it sees plaintext media. Calling that end-to-end encryption misleads users about who can access the call.
Persisting the next safe counter before use, or rotating after restart, are the two safe ways to avoid nonce reuse across crashes.
Lost packets are normal in real-time media; treating them as authentication failures or skipping authentication to recover would let attackers inject media. Loss is an availability issue only.
Non-overlapping key spaces ensure no two senders ever encrypt under the same key and nonce, which would break confidentiality and attribution.
Accepting old CTR values without a formally defined window lets attackers replay frames. A bounded window with proof of non-acceptance is the only safe exception.

Membership changes require the epoch to advance, all senders to rekey before resuming, keys to go only to the new set and new endpoints to receive no old keys; these together enforce join and leave confidentiality.
A departing or compromised device must not derive new-epoch secrets. Excluding it from the MLS epoch is how removal takes cryptographic effect.
Using an E2EESA pairwise or group profile for the media key control channel reuses analysed protection for key distribution instead of inventing a new channel.
A joining device should not hear the call from before it joined. Withholding prior-epoch key material enforces join confidentiality.
If the client cannot prove its counter continued correctly (e.g. after restore), reuse is possible; rotating to fresh keys removes the risk.
Keeping old epoch keys longer than the reordering window extends exposure if the device is later compromised. Discarding them bounds retention.
KID and context values are visible to the SFU; encoding meaningful data in them leaks information about participants or streams.
KID encoding must fit 64 bits; overflow could cause different senders or epochs to collide on the same KID.
SFrame is transport independent; allowing other transports is safe if all SFrame and E2EESA invariants are kept, avoiding WebRTC lock-in without weakening protection.
Because media is authenticated end-to-end, any SFU modification must cause authentication failure at endpoints, preventing undetected tampering.
Without both a time and a frame-count bound, keys could protect unbounded media, increasing exposure and approaching AEAD limits.
Some deployments must guarantee no participant can export plaintext media. Allowing policies to forbid bots supports that requirement.
Recorders and bots can read the call; if they are invisible, users wrongly believe only humans present can hear them.
Media must not resume under the old epoch after a membership change; otherwise removed members could still decrypt or new members be excluded inconsistently.
A compromised device in a live call keeps decrypting until removed and the epoch advances. Doing both before continuing limits ongoing exposure.
Encoded transforms apply SFrame inside the browser before media leaves the endpoint, which is necessary for E2EE in web clients.
Plaintext-capable services must be treated as participants with the same authorisation and visibility as people; otherwise they become hidden decryption paths.

Lifecycle states distinguish profiles safe by default from those needing explicit opt-in (provisional, experimental, legacy, deprecated). Defined states let resolvers keep risky profiles out unless deliberately chosen.
A new profile version can change security properties or dependencies. Treating a version change as a configuration change forces re-resolution so stale evaluation results are not carried forward.

Sender-key and fanout groups rely on a pairwise channel for key distribution; binding it to the consuming flow prevents an unrelated or weaker pairwise channel elsewhere from being counted as satisfying the dependency.
Family cardinality rules (e.g. exactly one identity architecture) prevent contradictory configurations; a violating set has no coherent security meaning and must fail.
Two versions of the same profile would make it ambiguous which rules apply, letting evaluators pick the weaker.
Account-root verification is only meaningful against the specific account-root identity profile in the same component; otherwise verification could refer to a different identity architecture.
Profiles legitimately depend on others (e.g. pairwise on identity). Exact references make the dependency unambiguous.
Conformance must be evaluated against a specific standard version and exact profiles; without them the result cannot be reproduced or compared.
Families address different concerns, so profiles from different families generally combine; explicit rules handle the exceptions.
Retaining resolution output with the artifact allows later reconstruction of which profiles actually applied, supporting audits and incident analysis.
Stable ordering makes serialized resolution output byte-identical across runs, which is needed for digests and comparison.
Individually recognised components may still conflict or lack required dependencies; conformance requires the combined configuration to satisfy all rules.
Ranges, floating tags and implicit upgrades let the evaluated configuration silently change. Exact pins keep conformance tied to a fixed set.
Non-deterministic dependency expansion would let two evaluators reach different effective sets and verdicts for the same input.

Content-protecting profiles are only secure with an identity architecture and secret storage bound in the same component; discharging host obligations explicitly prevents assuming they exist elsewhere.
Key transparency must refer to the same identity architecture and verification subject used by the component, otherwise it could prove consistency of a different subject.
Dependencies satisfied in another component or flow do not protect the consuming flow. Checking each flow and naming exact host obligations prevents cross-flow satisfaction.
Dependencies can add profiles to a family; allowing this keeps resolution complete while cardinality rules still apply.
Silently substituting a different architecture to repair a configuration would change security properties without the user's decision.
Choosing one of two conflicting required versions arbitrarily would break the other dependency's assumptions; failing exposes the conflict.
Required profiles must be included so the effective set actually contains everything the selected profiles depend on.
Cycles can be legitimate; requiring mutual satisfiability, exact pins, termination and no duplication keeps resolution safe and finite.
Typed dependency rules with explicit scope make component/flow binding machine-checkable instead of relying on prose.
Cardinality types encode whether a family is mandatory, optional or multi-valued, preventing missing or contradictory selections.
Explicit acceptance of non-default lifecycle states documents conscious risk acceptance rather than accidental use.

The listed failure conditions (unknown references, cardinality, incompatibility, version conflicts, unsatisfiable dependencies) each mean the configuration has no coherent meaning; failing prevents evaluating an incoherent set.
Attachments and sender-key media distribute keys over a parent channel; without binding an authenticated one in the same flow, keys could travel over an unauthenticated path.
Unknown references cannot be interpreted; guessing would evaluate against undefined rules.
If incompatibility were only one-directional, order of evaluation could let incompatible profiles coexist. Symmetry closes that gap.
Endpoint protocol profiles depend on client and transport security in the same component; without them, endpoint compromise or network attacks bypass protocol guarantees.
Representing competing approaches as distinct profiles in one family makes the choice explicit and comparable instead of baking one view into the standard.
Incompatibility declarations encode known unsafe or contradictory combinations so resolvers can reject them.
Prohibited profiles have known breaks; no opt-in may enable them.
Hidden dependency selection would change the effective configuration without the user or assessor seeing it.
Conformance results must be reproducible: the same input must yield the same effective set, warnings and outcome across conforming resolvers.
Listing property IDs from profiles shows intent, not implementation. Treating the union as proof would bypass evidence requirements.
Every reference must resolve in the catalog used; dangling references would leave parts of the configuration undefined.

Web clients load code from the server; binding all executable subresources and service-worker updates to the release manifest, with SRI and loader verification, prevents a server substituting malicious scripts.
Binding log entries to exact release digests, preventing checkpoint rollback and blocking releases on split views or failed witnesses lets clients refuse targeted malicious updates.
Closed schemas and content-addressed reports with identified assessor, policy, version and platform make client-security assessments reproducible and attributable.
Pinned HTTPS origin, secure context, HSTS, no mixed content and header-delivered CSP close the main paths by which web clients load attacker-controlled code.
Native clients must verify package signatures, use least privilege and sandboxing and disable debug features so that tampered builds or local attackers cannot easily read secrets.
Update metadata authenticated against independently provisioned roots and pinned signers prevents the update server from substituting releases or signers.
Platforms differ in security model; assessing each separately prevents a strong native result covering a weaker web build of the same product.
The reference engine checks records, not running clients or signatures. External assessors must perform those checks so engine output is not taken as runtime verification.
A verified-bootstrap verifier delivered by the same server it verifies would be trivially bypassed; installing it independently and covering all code paths makes verification meaningful.
The restrictive CSP (no default sources, hash-only scripts, no inline or eval) blocks script injection paths that would otherwise reach key material.
Origin and source checks, CSRF protection, frame isolation and no third-party scripts in secret contexts prevent cross-origin attacks from reaching keys or triggering actions.
A complete manifest of all executable artifacts with path, length and digest is the basis for verifying that clients run exactly the released code.
An append-only code log with verified proofs, persistent checkpoints, equivocation monitoring and independent witnesses makes targeted malicious releases detectable.
Update attacks include rollback, freeze, mix-and-match and partial installs; persisting accepted sequences and rejecting below-minimum versions defends against them.
Reasons for adverse or state-changing events explain decisions to applicants and auditors. Deleting them would let a certifier hide why a product was suspended or denied.
Separating evaluation from decision prevents one person both producing and approving the evidence, a basic conflict-of-interest control.
Allowing remediation before decision lets fixable findings be addressed instead of forcing denial, while keeping the event history explicit.
A successful appeal reopens review but must not itself certify; a fresh positive decision keeps certification tied to an evaluated outcome.
If terminal or adverse states could be edited away, revocations and denials would be meaningless. Only registered transitions may change state.
Entering renewal before expiry avoids certification gaps for products under continuing assessment.
Renewal must rest on current evidence; reusing stale evidence would certify a product version or configuration no longer evaluated.
Approving a bundle different from the one reviewed would certify unevaluated evidence; the digest must match exactly.
Revocation signals a serious problem; ordinary transitions reinstating it would undo revocation without a new full evaluation.
Expiring early could be used to drop a certification silently or mis-sequence events; expiry must follow the actual certificate time.
Surveillance lets certifiers re-examine certified products when concerns arise without waiting for renewal.
Applicants need a way to contest denials; appeal review provides it within the lifecycle rather than through record edits.
Declaring expected before and after states lets validators detect events applied out of order or against the wrong state.
Requiring from_state to equal the computed state prevents forked or replayed event histories.
Duplicate event IDs would allow replaying or ambiguously referencing events in the log.
An appeal decided by the person who made the original adverse decision is not an independent review.
New evidence cycles may replace the bundle, but naming the new digest explicitly keeps the chain of evidence auditable.
Surveillance after expiry would be meaningless; requiring the due date not exceed expiry keeps oversight within the certificate's life.
Out-of-order timestamps can disguise backdated decisions or reorder history.
Some programmes need stronger independence (separate organisations). Allowing later policy to add rules supports that without changing the base model.
Restricting events to registered transitions keeps the lifecycle a well-defined state machine with no undefined jumps.
A certificate past its surveillance due date without review has not been rechecked as required; presenting it as fully current would overstate assurance.
Due and expiry times earlier than the event make no sense and could be used to fabricate already-expired or overdue states.
The approving or denying actor must not have evaluated; this enforces separation of duties at the event level.
Applicants deciding their own certification is an obvious conflict of interest.
Suspended products are not currently certified; representing them otherwise would mislead relying parties.
The lowest assurance level (A1) does not require source access, matching its limited, black-box nature.
Evidence is scoped to properties; reusing evidence for an untested property would claim assurance that was never produced.
Exceptions are temporary risk acceptances; expiry forces re-evaluation instead of letting deviations persist indefinitely.
Evidence counted as independent assessment must come from an independent issuer; otherwise vendors could self-assess and present it as independent.
Each formal requirement must have its own evidence so formal coverage is complete and traceable.
Adding evidence types in later versions keeps the model extensible without reinterpreting existing bundles.
A claimed property supported only by not-supported records has no positive evidence; certifying it would be contradictory.
Higher assurance levels require source review because black-box testing cannot find many implementation flaws.
Exceptions must be fully described (scope, rationale, approver, expiry) so reviewers can judge and track accepted risk.
Binding the bundle to product, version, platform, configuration and plan prevents evidence being transplanted to another subject.
Waiving MUST requirements would let certification issue for non-conforming products.
One artifact can cover several requirements when it genuinely addresses them all, avoiding redundant evidence while staying honest about scope.
Evidence about behaviour without identified source or artifact scope cannot be tied to the certified product.
Each claimed property needs at least one evidence record; otherwise claims are unsupported assertions.
Named independent assessors who produced no evidence suggest their participation was nominal.
Evidence about a different build or source does not demonstrate the assessed subject's behaviour.
Categories are a floor; certification policies may require more evidence for higher risk products.
Reusing a bundle for another version, platform or configuration certifies something never evaluated.
The listed validator failures (missing bindings, unsupported claims, expired exceptions, wrong scope) are the conditions under which the bundle cannot support certification.
Exceptions may only cover SHOULD deviations or narrowing limitations; this keeps MUST requirements non-waivable.
Vendor artifacts are useful context but not independent; counting them as independent would undermine assurance levels.
Declaring source-access mode sets which evidence types are valid and what assessors could see.
Evidence dated after the observation time could not have been considered and suggests backdating or tampering.
Different envelope formats must not change meaning; identical payload digests ensure JOSE and COSE copies attest the same thing.
Binding each status to its predecessor makes the status history a chain, so verifiers can detect omitted or forked statements.
Signatures over non-canonical JSON can verify differently across parsers; canonicalisation ensures all verifiers check the same bytes.
An attestation must rest on a valid evidence bundle; issuing without validation would certify unsupported claims.
Rendering not-supported as certified would claim protection that the evaluation explicitly did not find.
Envelope headers outside the signed payload could change interpretation without invalidating signatures.
Fixed ASCII keys, valid Unicode and no floats remove encoding ambiguities that could make the same payload hash differently.
Dropping limitations from conditional claims would present them as unconditional certification.
Certification can be revoked after issuance; consumers must check a current signed status statement in the listed cases to avoid relying on stale certificates.
Status statements must bind the latest event, full event log, current bundle and not outlive the certificate, so status cannot be detached from the lifecycle.
Accepting a lower sequence would let an attacker replay an older status, e.g. before revocation.
Signatures must use registered, non-prohibited algorithms for new issuance so attestations are not forgeable with weak algorithms.
The signing backend requirements (key protection, access control, audit) protect the attestation keys whose compromise would allow forged certifications.
Inventing private algorithm identifiers would break interoperability and could collide with future standard ones; RFC 9964 identifiers must be used.
Threshold signatures over different bytes would not jointly attest the same statement.
Suspended, revoked or expired status means the product is not currently certified; verification must fail.
Attestation claims must match the validated bundle and assurance plan, so signed statements cannot claim more than was evaluated.
Replaying an old certified statement after a newer adverse one would reinstate certification without authority.
Automated assessments may use any permitted model, but probability claims carry a stronger meaning that requires calibration.
An uncalibrated score is not a probability; calling it one misleads consumers about how often classifications are correct.
Reconstructing model, version, inputs and thresholds lets reviewers audit automated classifications and reproduce them.
When human and automated assessments agree, declaring which supplies the final confidence avoids hidden averaging that would produce a value neither assessor gave.
Calibration evaluated after the assessment could not have informed it and suggests backdating.
needs-review records are unresolved; giving them final labels would present undecided items as decided.
Recording the classifier's identity, version and parameters allows auditing and detecting drift between versions.
For mixed policies, final classifications require human and automated agreement to avoid one silently overriding the other.
Stale calibration may no longer reflect classifier behaviour; enforcing the maximum age keeps probability claims current.
A rationale tying evidence to the confidence level makes human judgements reviewable rather than arbitrary.
Without a maximum calibration age, very old calibration could justify current probabilities.
Revisions must preserve history and link to predecessors so classifications cannot be silently rewritten.
Deleting source assessments after resolution would remove the evidence for how a final decision was reached.
Mapping qualitative human judgements to numbers without a documented mapping invents false precision.
Binding subject, labels, confidence, assessors and policy to each record prevents classifications being moved between subjects or policies.
In consensus mode, mismatched labels mean no consensus; finalising would misrepresent agreement.
Mixed or weighted disagreement cannot be resolved automatically without hiding one view; sending to review keeps disagreement visible.
Describing automated results as human-reviewed overstates the scrutiny they received.
STIX confidence is an ordinal scale, not a probability; silent conversion invents a calibrated meaning.
Comparing human and automated assessments requires a common scale; both must use STIX 0-100 in that mode.
Humans do not produce calibrated probabilities; labelling their judgements that way is misleading.
Representing reviewers as person agents gives provenance that distinguishes humans from software agents.
Raw model scores in [0,1] are not calibrated probabilities; the label requires calibration evidence.
A classified record without labels or confidence has no content, so classification must carry both.
Without the version prefix, tools may misparse a v4 vector as v3 and compute the wrong severity.
A product both fixed and affected for the same vulnerability gives consumers contradictory patch guidance.
Validation warnings flag questionable advisory content; dropping them hides issues from consumers.
Advisory updates must increment version, record revision history and keep identifiers so consumers can see what changed and trust they are reading the latest version.
A fixed product without a matching affected product in scope makes the fix claim unverifiable and may mislead users of other branches.
Down-converting v4 to v3 loses information and can change severity, misrepresenting risk.
KEV lists only confirmed known exploitation; absence does not mean unexploited, and treating it so delays urgent patching.
Internal exploitation findings and KEV come from different evidence; forcing agreement would discard real signals.
CSAF 2.0 cannot carry all modern metrics; summarising them in notes keeps information visible while the normalised record remains authoritative.
The internal exporter checks semantics, not full CSAF validity; claiming csaf_validated would overstate conformance.
An immutable fix reference lets consumers obtain exactly the remediated artifact rather than a moving target.
Vulnerabilities can involve several weakness classes; recording all aids root-cause analysis.
PURL and CPE help automated matching of affected products in inventories.
Remediations must state which products they apply to so users know whether a fix is relevant.
Malformed CVE IDs break cross-referencing with other databases.
Publishing a score without the full vector and version prevents verification of how it was computed.
KEV observations change over time; recording source, time and status preserves provenance for later review.
Consistent CWE formatting enables reliable mapping to the CWE catalogue.
CWE classifies weaknesses, not specific vulnerabilities; using it as an identifier conflates distinct issues.
Refreshing time-varying signals without rewriting history keeps an auditable record of what was known when.
Human-readable representation is allowed, but the normalised record stays authoritative so machine consumers are not misled by prose.
Waiting for a normal release train could leave users exposed past the disclosure deadline or during active exploitation.
Old versions still in use remain vulnerable; guidance helps users mitigate or migrate.
Distinguishing report receipt, triage, confirmation, remediation and disclosure keeps handling state accurate for deadlines and audits.
Consistent CVSS v4 recording, or a justified exception, gives a comparable severity baseline.
Recording why a report was rejected allows later review and prevents silent dismissal of real issues.
Identifying affected products, versions and severity before remediation ensures fixes target the right scope.
SSVC trees differ by stakeholder and version; recording the exact tree makes decisions reproducible.
Duplicates must not reset deadlines; otherwise re-reports could be used to delay disclosure indefinitely.
Root causes enable systemic fixes; restating symptoms leaves the underlying flaw unaddressed.
Active exploitation requires prompt escalation; the escalation must happen within the defined clock.
Duplicate records need links to the original and reporter information so credit and history are preserved.
New evidence can show a rejected report was valid; reopening without erasing events keeps the history honest.
Closing a case must not hide accepted risks still outstanding.
Accepting risk on an actively exploited vulnerability leaves users under attack; such cases need remediation or mitigation.
A remedy must be tested, available and documented before disclosure so users can act on the advisory.
Stating per supported version whether it will be fixed, mitigated or not fixed informs users of their options.
Emergency response records (who, when, actions) support accountability and post-incident review.
Postmortems for critical or exploited cases capture lessons and systemic fixes.
Inventing a separate disclosure deadline would conflict with the policy-defined clock.
Multi-vendor issues require coordination; recording participants supports it.
Adding vendors must not reset dates; otherwise coordination could be used to delay disclosure.
Active exploitation demands emergency handling; anything less would leave users exposed.
These obligations (severity, scope, plan, deadlines) define the minimum complete handling for confirmed vulnerabilities.
Exploitation and context change urgency; hiding them in a static base score understates risk.
Shared components affect many vendors; policies must support coordination to avoid partial fixes.
The listed policy elements (scope, contact, safe harbor, deadlines, coordination) are the minimum for researchers to report safely and know what to expect.
Extensions are allowed only under recorded justified conditions, preventing indefinite delays.
Deadlines must be positive and bounded; 180 days caps how long users remain uninformed.
Safe-harbor statements encourage good-faith research without fear of legal action.
security.txt Contact and Expires are required by RFC 9116 so researchers can reach the right team and trust the information is current.
Deadline extensions need a real dependency, recorded reason and advance notice to the reporter to keep the process fair and accountable.
Resetting the clock when vendors join would allow coordination to postpone disclosure indefinitely.
Trusted coordinators help manage multi-party disclosure and conflicts.
Researchers encountering sensitive data must stop, minimise retention and report, protecting affected users.
Defining prohibited conduct (e.g. DoS, social engineering, data exfiltration) sets clear boundaries for authorised research.
Explicit deadlines per severity tier give predictable disclosure timing.
Earlier disclosure by mutual agreement can benefit users when fixes are ready.
Severe issues should be disclosed no later than minor ones; inverse ordering would delay critical warnings.
Disclosing 30 days after a fix gives users time to patch while capping delay at day 120.
Requiring account identifiers would deter anonymous reporters and leak reporter identity.
Declared policy parameters (scope, channels, deadlines) make the policy machine-checkable and transparent.
Using v4.0 with full vectors makes published scores verifiable and comparable.
Exploited reports need rapid escalation (24h) and a decision on warnings within 72h to protect users.
Short expiry ensures security.txt is reviewed regularly and contact data stays current.
Rotating a backup credential cannot reach copies an attacker already holds (old ciphertext, wraps, snapshots). Claiming revocation of those would give users false assurance after a credential leak.
A local vault password change and a server-hosted backup credential rotation face different attackers and authorities; conflating them would apply the wrong guarantees.
The reference script checks digests and checkpoint freshness structurally; stating its limits prevents the structural pass being taken as cryptographic proof of rotation.
A fresh 256-bit BDEK per generation ensures a credential rotation actually changes the content key, so old keys do not decrypt new data.
The central rotation claim is that old credentials cannot open new generations; only an actual negative decrypt test demonstrates it.
Client-authorised versioned transitions between exact manifests prevent the server from performing or replaying rotations itself.
Arrays carry meaning in order; only schema-declared sets may be sorted, and duplicates rejected, so digests cannot be changed or collided by reordering.
Restricting RFC 8785 to integers in the safe range and no floats removes cross-language numeric ambiguity that could make signatures verify differently.
Reinterpreting historical signed bytes under the active scheme could make old signatures verify for different content; explicit scheme identity prevents this.
Converting decimal scores to binary floats loses precision and can change values; keeping exact decimal strings preserves source fidelity.
Product classes may need fewer algorithms; narrowing reduces attack surface without changing the shared registry.
Recording the exact registry version lets conformance results be reproduced against the algorithm set that existed at evaluation time.
A suite is only as strong as its weakest component; labelling it stronger would overstate assurance.
The listed invalid registry states (duplicates, unknown statuses, missing reasons, prohibited members) would make lifecycle decisions unreliable.
Registering experimental or research algorithms documents them without endorsing their use.
A PQ algorithm in the registry does not make a product PQ-secure; claims still need the property model and profile requirements.
Prohibited components or overstated suite status would allow broken algorithms inside approved suites.
Lifecycle categories communicate how algorithms may be used, from preferred defaults to prohibited.
Inventing primitives is a major source of cryptographic failure; relying on reviewed standards avoids it.
Hybrid TLS groups are specific named constructions; treating arbitrary component pairs as equivalent would carry unanalysed claims.
Exact identifiers prevent implementations substituting unregistered or similarly named algorithms.
Lifecycle status governs permitted use, not security of an arbitrary combination; robustness must be argued per construction.
Migrations that keep old algorithms negotiable create a path for attackers to force the deprecated option.
When an algorithm is broken, waiting for multi-party governance prolongs exposure; a single designated authority may stop new use.
Stopping use of a broken asset can be safer than continuing even without a replacement, accepting temporary unavailability.
Silent fallback to the affected asset would undo the emergency migration.
Credible emergencies must be stoppable quickly; governance delays would leave users exposed.
Union payloads and external formats are ambiguous; explicit integration contracts prevent the same bytes being interpreted under different schemas.
Trying both active and historical encodings lets an attacker pick whichever verifies, enabling cross-scheme confusion.
Binding algorithm and profile into the signature input prevents signatures being transplanted between algorithms or profiles.
Exact digest contracts specify included and excluded fields, preventing digests silently covering different data.
Ciphertext may pass through relays when encryption, key binding and recipients are explicit, so routing does not count as disclosure.
Public data and business processing are not E2EE content; misclassifying them inflates or obscures protection claims.
Content-derived data sent to non-recipients defeats E2EE; only explicit, authenticated, user-initiated, finite disclosures are allowed.
Without independently verified, source-bound egress evidence, protected-content claims cannot be confirmed and must stay indeterminate.
Binding claims to components, flows, endpoint identities, key fingerprints and transport makes egress claims precise and testable.
The evaluator inspects structured observations, not raw traffic or memory; stating this prevents its output being treated as full egress verification.
Classifiers, embeddings, previews, hashes and indexes derived from content leak it as surely as plaintext; all must be treated as protected.
A closed set of coarse codes and fields limits what telemetry can reveal.
Binding evidence to policy and product and testing for leakage, consent and retention shows telemetry behaves as claimed.
Every release consumes privacy budget; recording all in an authenticated ledger and capping lifetime epsilon keeps the DP guarantee valid.
Default-off, revocable consent and no core-function dependence ensure users are not coerced into sharing diagnostics.
Coarse data can still identify users; calling it anonymous without DP or unlinkability proof misleads users.
Excluding content, keys, identifiers, contacts, URLs and precise timestamps prevents telemetry becoming a side channel for protected data.
Defining the privacy unit as a user's lifetime contribution with bounded per-query contribution is necessary for a meaningful DP guarantee.
A seven-day retention bound and authenticated encrypted access limit exposure of diagnostic data.
A minimum of 20 contributors per release reduces risk from small cohorts, but is explicitly not the DP guarantee.
Services that only handle ciphertext and hold no content keys or authorisation roots cannot read or impersonate users even if compromised.
