Login and storage credentials are held or resettable by the provider; letting them add devices would make the provider able to eavesdrop.
Content-addressed, assessor-identified reports bound to policy and product make server-trust assessments reproducible.
Plaintext-receiving bots are endpoints; making them visible and separately authorised prevents hidden decryption paths.
Opaque locators with bounded times and client-authorised recipients prevent storage records leaking identities or being redirected.
Server-side disk encryption with server keys is not E2EE; content must stay application-encrypted across TLS terminators and storage.
Bounded ciphertext retention (≤30 days) limits how much stored data a breach or harvest-now attacker can collect.
An explicit metadata allowlist with encryption at rest limits what the server can reveal about communication patterns.
A complete inventory of components, subprocessors and privileged capabilities is needed to find every path that could reach content or keys.
Recomputing digests and authenticating them under independent roots, with isolated signing credentials, ensures users install exactly the signed release.
Hermetic pinned builds reproduced byte-identically by an independent operator detect a compromised build system.
Signing thresholds must count distinct trusted identities; duplicates from one identity would let a single compromised key meet the threshold.
A validated SBOM bound to the release lets users find vulnerable components in exactly what they run.
Standard in-toto/SLSA provenance in authenticated DSSE envelopes lets verifiers check how artifacts were built with interoperable tools.
Rejecting dirty checkouts, path escapes and symlinks prevents unreviewed files entering builds; pinned toolchains make reproductions comparable.
The attested-reproducible profile ties release bytes to source, inputs, builder, signing policy and reproduction, giving end-to-end provenance.
A closed SLSA subset binding one subject, authorised builder and canonical source prevents ambiguous or permissive provenance.
SLSA L2 requires hosted builds with authenticated provenance; L3 claims need hardened builders. Stating levels prevents overclaiming.
Complete inventories including transitive and CI inputs are needed to assess supply-chain exposure.
Binding assessments to product, policy and source inventory makes approvals and gate results traceable to exact code.
Independent review and dual release authorisation prevent a single developer introducing and shipping malicious or flawed changes.
Bounded fuzzing with preserved failures and pinned scanners gives reproducible evidence that parsers and dependencies were tested.
Open findings block release until fixed with retests or properly accepted, preventing known vulnerabilities from shipping.
Required passing checks with immutable tool identities ensure gates actually ran on the release.
All baseline controls apply; even teams without app packages must assess runtime and build dependencies.
Security-relevant changes require updating threat models and tests so documentation reflects the current design.
Only medium/low risks may be accepted, by independent reviewers with documented rationale and controls, keeping risk acceptance accountable.
Isolating untrusted PRs from release secrets and protecting branches prevents attackers stealing signing keys via CI.
Mapping controls to all SSDF practice areas with owners and evidence ensures coverage and accountability.
Fuzz evidence bound to targets, corpus, tool, duration and counts shows fuzzing was meaningful and reproducible.
External tests must use real interfaces and hostile peers, and internal review must inspect trust boundaries and key lifecycle, to find realistic flaws.
Black-box testing cannot observe internal properties like state erasure or build provenance; such claims need white-box evidence.
Failed, skipped or flaky results are not coverage; counting them would inflate assurance. Counterexamples become regression tests.
Explicit profiles and independent, authenticated, complete assessment prevent self-assessment or partial testing being presented as verification.
Pointing to related standards sections clarifies how verification fits with formal methods, assurance tiers and certification, avoiding duplicate or conflicting rules.
Resolving policy through the profile engine with exact versions ensures verification targets the same configuration conformance evaluates.
Adversarial suites covering downgrade, replay and unauthorised enrolment test the threats the standard claims to defend against.
Binding suites to source, artifacts, method, profiles, properties, tools and assessor makes results attributable and reproducible.
Standard primitives can still be implemented incorrectly; claims about the product need proof that the implementation corresponds to the analysed design.
Assurance profiles describe how claims are checked, not what the architecture provides; using them as the basis for a claim would let assurance substitute for the actual mechanism.
Duplicate assessor IDs blur who produced which evidence and can inflate independence counts.
The resolver steps (exact resolution, obligation derivation, level checks) make assurance plans deterministic and complete.
Assurance profiles depend on verification and formal profiles; unresolved dependencies would leave required evidence undefined.
A5 requires computational proofs for properties like confidentiality; deriving obligations ensures they are actually produced.
Higher assurance levels must be strictly stronger; dropping lower-level requirements would make a higher label weaker.
A1 is black-box only and cannot speak to internal key lifecycle or build integrity; using it to imply those would overclaim.
Claimed properties must come from architecture profiles actually configured; otherwise the plan would assure properties the product does not implement.
A3 protocol properties require symbolic formal obligations so protocol-level claims are backed by formal analysis.
